text:
I've written the spec for #5508 and filed it as **#5511** (the spec: an adopter's lander picks Actions or local by its median run, with a local fallback). It is a sub-issue of #5508 and carries `kind:spec` and `takes:to-tickets`. It is assigned to this session, as the repo's rules have `/to-spec` do. I relabelled #5508 from `takes:to-spec` to `takes:children` and released my claim on it. I edited no repo file and committed nothing.

**What the spec settles**

- **How the tester is picked.** `landingTester` gets a new value, `auto`, which becomes the default for adopters. At each lander launch, the lander takes the median suite time of the newest 20 whole runs in `.lander-runs.jsonl`, counting both local and Actions runs. Over 3 min, that run tests on Actions; otherwise it tests locally. With fewer than 5 runs it tests locally. workflow-core keeps its `actions` setting and nothing changes for it.
- **The local fallback.** Three cases hand an ask to the local tester:
  - a run whose failed jobs never started a step, which is how a budget block shows up;
  - no run listed once the existing 3-minute wait passes;
  - `gh` refusing a call for any reason other than a network fault.

  A red on the code stays a red. To make the fallback safe, the adopter Actions tester takes one ask at a time and runs no pre-commit gates, like the local tester. That choice is logged on #5511 as a delegated decision.
- **The workflows.** Core will write two lander workflows into every adopter on `auto`, marked as core-owned so each upgrade rewrites them: one runs the whole suite on push to the `lander/*` suite refs, the other reruns named files. They keep the job names the Actions tester already reads. Each shard job runs the same group of tests as the local whole run. They run on `ubuntu-24.04-arm` unless the `ci` key names a runner, with a 15-minute job timeout by default.
- **#5343's ruling.** Its "push to `main` only, never a `lander/*` ref" no longer holds for lander refs, overridden by #5468 Q2 (B) (the founder's choice of the run-length rule). The spec covers rewriting the docs that still say it.
- **Tests.** Each piece is tested where existing tests already drive it: the lander's tester wiring, the Actions tester with stubbed `gh` reads, and the file writer that writes the core-owned workflows.

**Still unchecked:** nobody has confirmed that the token has Actions write access on the adopter repos. If it doesn't, the fallback keeps those landings local. The spec has the build check this on design-vault once it is public, and report the result.

**Values the spec relies on:** the 3-minute threshold, the 20-run and 5-run counts, the 15-minute timeout and the named-rerun cap of 12 a day are all untraced. `auto` as the default rests on #5468's ruling.

**Practice:** covered — test-and-ci-performance, Researched 2026-10-22.

Sources for how a budget-blocked job looks:
- [GitHub community discussion 166876](https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/166876)
- [proteinlens CI/CD budget exhaustion](https://lucaberton.com/blog/proteinlens-ci-cd-budget-exhaustion/)

**Next:** run `/to-tickets 5511`. Separately, item 3 in #5463's ranked list (the map these changes come from) still says #5508 "takes `/to-spec`". I left the map's body as it is.

I've closed #5185, the ticket asking whether test queue wait belongs in the spec. I made the call myself rather than asking you: once I checked what admission was doing, the answer was clear.

**Decision:** the spec reports queue wait alongside total closes per hour, as two figures: the share of session time spent queued, and how much wait each added session brings. It has no threshold and doesn't feed admission.

- **Daily wait since #4956 landed** (#4956 is the admission change for Windows memory): 17.7 h on 11 Nov, 33.8 h on 12 Nov, and 20.7 h on 13 Nov up to 17:30 UTC. - **Why it doesn't become a session limit:** in the busiest-waiting hours, admission was already at its ceiling 88% of the time, held there by memory limits that #4962 confirmed. A queue-wait rule would only act in the other 12%, counting the same memory pressure twice. Going lower would need proof that a waiting session costs closes, and #4160 showed closes can't detect that. #5184 turned down an adaptive CPU limit for the same reason.
- **Your 10 Nov question** (should frequent memory-held tests lower the session count?): not on queue wait. The memory limits already hold the count in most high-wait hours. The per-session figure the spec reports is what any later rethink would go on.

This is recorded as a delegated decision on #5185, with the resolution comment and a new line in the map's Decisions so far on #3209 (the throughput map). If you'd rather have a queue-wait limit on sessions, a new ticket on #3209 can add one; nothing has been built.
